clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant tubulopathy characterised by hypertension with hyperkalaemia and hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis in the presence of a normal glomerular filtration rate.
Plasma renin is suppressed and aldosterone is inappropriately low or normal for the degree of hyperkalaemia.
It is caused by mutations in WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 or CUL3 that increase activity of the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule.
It is essentially the mirror image of Gitelman syndrome and characteristically shows a dramatic response to thiazide diuretics at low doses.
Hyperkalaemia occurs despite normal kidney function and without potassium-sparing drugs, which is an important diagnostic clue.
Hypercalciuria and reduced bone density may occur, and dental abnormalities with short stature are seen particularly with CUL3 mutations.
Recessive KLHL3 mutations and CUL3 mutations tend to produce a more severe, earlier-onset phenotype.
It should be considered in any young person with unexplained hyperkalaemia and hypertension.
reference.pathophysiology: The with-no-lysine kinases WNK1 and WNK4 regulate the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule through the downstream SPAK and OSR1 kinases. KLHL3 and CUL3 assemble a Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase that normally targets the WNK kinases for degradation. Disease-causing mutations, whether intronic changes that increase WNK1 expression, WNK4 mutations, or KLHL3 and CUL3 mutations that impair WNK degradation, all raise WNK signalling and NCC activity and so enhance electroneutral sodium-chloride reabsorption. The resulting extracellular volume expansion causes hypertension and suppresses renin, while reduced sodium delivery to the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron and loss of the lumen-negative driving force impair potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. Because the defect amplifies the very transporter that thiazides inhibit, the condition is exquisitely thiazide-responsive.
additionalDifferentials: Type IV renal tubular acidosis and hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, including the diabetic form
Adrenal insufficiency and pseudohypoaldosteronism type I
Drug-induced hyperkalaemia (renin-angiotensin blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, calcineurin inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs)
Primary aldosteronism and other causes of secondary hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium, chloride and bicarbonate with a venous or arterial blood gas
Renal function and estimated glomerular filtration rate to confirm it is preserved
Exclusion of adrenal insufficiency and review of the medication list
Molecular genetic testing of WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 and CUL3 with family screening
redFlags: Severe hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes and arrhythmia risk
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent with treatment: thiazide diuretics typically normalise blood pressure, serum potassium and the acidosis; left untreated, the sustained hypertension carries the usual long-term cardiovascular risk.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as type IV renal tubular acidosis or chronic kidney disease
Attributing the hyperkalaemia to drugs and halting the search for a unifying diagnosis
Overlooking the characteristic diagnostic and therapeutic response to thiazide diuretics
Failing to screen affected family members
Relying on indiscriminate potassium-lowering measures instead of targeting the underlying transporter defect
references: Brenner and Rector's The Kidney (standard reference)
management: Use a low-dose thiazide diuretic as first-line therapy, which characteristically corrects the hypertension, hyperkalaemia and hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
Advise dietary sodium and potassium restriction to support control of volume expansion and hyperkalaemia
Monitor serum potassium, chloride, bicarbonate and blood pressure to titrate treatment and confirm the response
Undertake surveillance for hypercalciuria and reduced bone density, with dental review particularly in CUL3-related disease
Perform molecular genetic testing of WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 and CUL3 with family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
Provide nephrology follow-up and long-term cardiovascular risk management for the sustained hypertension
